## Accessibility

I care a lot about making the things I create, whether they are visualizations or applications, usable by as many people as possible. Accessibility is part of responsible science communication! This page outlines the practices I follow and the areas where I’m continuing to learn and improve.

## Feedback

If you run into any accessibility barriers on my site or in the materials I share, I genuinely want to know. Please open an issue in my [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mmorenorolon/mmorenorolon.github.io/issues) and I’ll do my best to address it promptly.

Thank you for taking the time to visit and read this page. <i class="fa-solid fa-heart"></i>

## Accessibility Practices

This site is designed with the following considerations in mind:

- Color contrast that meets WCAG 2.1 AA standards.  

I rely on a palette that stays readable across devices and lighting conditions, and I’m intentional about avoiding color combinations that can make maps or plots hard to interpret.

- Alternative text for all informative images.  

When I include figures or graphics, I aim for alt text that communicates the meaning of the visualization—not just what it looks like.

- Readable, accessible typography.  

I use Red Hat Text because it avoids impostor letter shapes and tends to be more comfortable for readers with dyslexic traits or low vision.

- Clear structure for longer content.  

Blog posts include a sidebar table of contents to make navigation easier, especially for screen reader users or anyone skimming for specific sections.

- Accessible scientific content.

Since I often share maps, plots, and code:

- Legends avoid color-only encoding when possible

- Code blocks use consistent spacing and readable font sizes

- Tables include proper headers for screen readers

- Jargon is minimized or explained when it appears

I’m still learning how to build more inclusive and accessible digital content. I’m not a web developer, but I regularly audit my site and update things as I discover better practices. These are the tools I use most often:

- [WAVE Web Accessibility Evaluation Tool](https://wave.webaim.org/)

I document any issues I find and the steps I take to fix them in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mmorenorolon/mmorenorolon.github.io) that houses this site.
